section.title: Introduction and Overview
section.p: eXML is a RISC OS module which adds support for the XML file format to applications written in any language, including BBC BASIC. Existing ports of XML libraries have generally been C sources written by others, optimised for the C language, and not straightforward to call from other languages; some have also been withdrawn by their authors. eXML exists to give RISC OS software a single, dependable set of SWI calls for creating and parsing XML documents, without requiring a C compiler or a callback-based programming style.

Only a subset of the full XML specification is implemented. The intention is to extend coverage over time, but this is not guaranteed, and several calls described in this chapter are only partially implemented or not yet implemented at all; each such call says so explicitly.

subsection.title: Approach
subsection.p: Most existing XML libraries rely heavily on callbacks and handlers: the main program registers functions that the parser calls when it recognises something of interest. This is a natural style in C or C++, but it does not suit simpler languages such as BBC BASIC.

eXML instead follows the same pattern as the RISC OS window manager. The application calls with the appropriate parameters, and the call exits with a return code describing what was found. Once the application has dealt with that return code, it calls again, and repeats this until it receives the Finished code, at which point it resumes the normal flow of the program.

When handling long XML files, it may be desirable to call Wimp_Poll frequently from within the parsing loop. Take care when doing this: another running task may not be aware that your program is still in the middle of parsing a document.

subsection.title: Encodings
subsection.p: Several character encodings can be used for the data in a document. The eXML calls refer to these encodings by a fixed number:

Not every listed encoding is necessarily implemented in the current release of the module: selecting an unsupported encoding produces the UnknownEncoding result code from . Until wider encoding support is confirmed, use the standard Latin-1 encoding (2) for documents. UTF-8, in particular, though ASCII-compatible and defined in Unicode, ISO 10646-1 and RFC 2279, is not currently supported.
Reserved characters are escaped transparently on both read and write, so calling code does not need to handle this itself:

subsection.title: Workspace and the element stack
subsection.p: The workspace used by the eXML module must be supplied by the calling application, rather than being owned by the module itself. This allows the module to be replaced by a newer version at any time without disturbing running applications, and allows several programs (or several independent parts of one program) to run concurrently, each with its own workspace and its own preferences. For example, a C or Assembler program expects strings to be terminated with a 0x00 byte, whereas BBC BASIC expects a 0x0D (Carriage Return) terminator; because each caller supplies its own workspace, each can select the terminator it needs without affecting any other caller.

Within the supplied workspace, eXML keeps a stack of currently open elements, fixed at 1024 bytes. Each element that is opened is pushed onto this stack as a null-terminated string, and the module maintains pointers to the current element. This lets the module track the order in which elements are opened and closed, report an error if it finds an inconsistency (for example, elements closed out of order), and, when writing, close any elements you have left open without you having to name them individually.

subsection.title: The module name 'eXML'
subsection.p: The module is called eXML, pronounced "ex-em-el", in the same way as the abbreviation XML. The extra leading e exists because SWI names cannot begin with the letter X: that letter is reserved as a prefix which suppresses a SWI's normal error handling. To trap errors from an eXML call yourself, prefix its name with X in the usual way, for example SYS "XeXML_StartElement", ....

subsection.title: Library
subsection.p: A BBC BASIC library is supplied in the !eXML application folder. Place this folder somewhere the Filer sees at start-up, such as inside !Boot.Resources, so that programs using the library can find it.

section.title: Technical Details
section.p: eXML offers a set of SWI calls that any application can use to create and parse XML files. Because the module can be dynamically replaced, and each caller supplies its own workspace, each application (or each routine within an application) can hold its own set of preferences to be honoured by eXML independently of any other caller.

Before eXML can be used, the application must reserve a block of memory of suitable size for the workspace. The application requests the required size by calling with a null pointer, then calls it again with a pointer to the newly claimed memory to initialise it to sensible defaults. Preferences are then set with ; for example, textual strings returned by the module are terminated with a 0x00 byte by default, which suits C or Assembler, but BASIC needs a 0x0D (Carriage Return) terminator instead, and is used to change this.

The available calls fall into four groups, described in the four SWI Calls sections below: calls to initialise the XML workspace, calls to read (parse) an XML file, calls to write an XML file, and universal calls that are not specifically tied to XML parsing or writing.

category.title: Attribute array
category.p: When reports a StartElement or Declaration, or when supplying attributes to , , or , attributes are held as an array of pairs of pointers: a pointer to the attribute's name, followed by a pointer to its value. The array is terminated by a null pointer. For example, the element
A pointer to an attribute array is 0 (rather than a valid pointer to an empty array) whenever no attributes were found, or none are to be supplied.

category.title: Context array and context string
category.p: On exit from , R3 normally points to a zero-terminated array of word pointers, one per currently open element, in the order the elements were opened - the path from the document root down to (but not including) the element currently being processed. If, for example, an element is opened while the parser is at document/chapter/page, the context array on exit looks like this:

If bit 0 of the flags word is set on entry to , R3 instead points to a single context string using the current element separator (see ), for example /document/chapter/page, rather than to an array of pointers. The name of the element currently being opened or closed is not included in either form of context, because at that point it is not yet (or is no longer) part of the context; append it yourself if you need the full path, eg. context$ = context$ + "/" + $element%. produces the string form of the context on demand, at any point, without needing bit 0 of the flags word to have been set.

category.title: Colour data block
category.p: reads and writes colour values through a fixed-size, fixed-format data block held in memory supplied by the caller - either a short-lived block used purely for one conversion, or part of a larger structure holding several colours or other parameters. Always request the required size first (see ), since it may grow in a future version of the module.

offset-table.offset: Bit flags; not used at present
The original colour model used (RGB, CMYK, HSV, YUV); see below
The original format (syntax) used to define the colour; see below
The colour, always as a RISC OS colour word (see below)
The colour in its original colour model
Name of the colour, if it was a named colour, including terminator

category.p: The Model field is stored purely for reference, for example so that your software can preselect an appropriate colour model in a colour picker matching how the colour was originally specified.
The colour Value is always held as a RISC OS colour word, &BBGGRRtt: one byte each for blue, green and red, and a trailing transparency byte (0 for fully opaque, 255 for fully transparent).
Colour format numbers, used both to report the format a colour was read in and to select the format written by :

value-table.value: Default - use the format already recorded in the data block
Name - a named HTML colour, eg. white, yellow, green

category.p: The full set of named HTML colours recognised is: white, yellow, orange, red, fuchsia, silver, gray, olive, purple, maroon, aqua, lime, teal, green, blue, navy, black. Names are not case-sensitive, and their use is discouraged in favour of an explicit RGB value wherever possible.

section.title: SWI Calls: Initialising the XML Workspace
section.p: The SWI calls are grouped, across this section and the three that follow it, as they are in the original specification: calls to initialise the XML workspace, calls to read (parse) an XML file, calls to write an XML file, and universal calls used by both directions (or unrelated to parsing altogether).

swi-definition.name: eXML_InitBuffer
swi-definition.description: Reserve and initialise the XML workspace, with a configurable Content buffer

entry.register-use: pointer to workspace in the application's own memory, or 0 to request the required size
required size, in bytes, of the Content buffer

exit.register-use: required size of the workspace, in bytes (when R0 was 0 on entry)

use.p: Call this SWI twice. First, with a null pointer in R0, to discover the required workspace size; then, having claimed a block of that size, call it again with a pointer to that block in R0. The second call clears the block to zero and fills in sensible default preferences. The resulting pointer (R0 on the second call) must be passed in R0 to every other eXML SWI for that session.
R1 gives the required size of the Content buffer used to hold parsed content data; the module imposes a minimum of 1KB if a smaller value (or a null pointer) is supplied.
This call supersedes and should be used in its place.

p.extended-example: content_size% = 10*1024 SYS "eXML_InitBuffer",0,content_size%,,,,0 TO size% DIM xml% size% SYS "eXML_InitBuffer",xml%,content_size%

swi-definition.name: eXML_Init
swi-definition.description: Deprecated: reserve and initialise the XML workspace with a fixed-size Content buffer

entry.register-use: pointer to workspace in the application's own memory, or 0 to request the required size

exit.register-use: required size of the workspace, in bytes (when R0 was 0 on entry)

use.p: This call is deprecated, and is supplied only for backwards compatibility. It assumes a fixed size for the Content buffer (10KB from version 0.18 onwards; 1KB in older versions). allows the Content buffer size to be chosen and should be used in preference to this call.
As with , call this SWI twice: once with a null pointer in R0 to discover the required size, and once with a pointer to a claimed block of that size to initialise it.

p.extended-example: SYS "eXML_Init" TO size% DIM xml% size% FOR dummy% = 0 TO size% STEP 4 xml%!dummy% = 0 NEXT SYS "eXML_Init",xml%

swi-definition.name: eXML_SetOption
swi-definition.description: Set a configurable preference for a workspace

entry.register-use: new value, or pointer to a string, as appropriate to the selected variable

use.p: Once initialised, eXML uses sensible default values for every configurable preference. This call changes one of them for the workspace given in R0. The variable number in R1 behaves as a reason code, selecting which preference is changed and how R2 is interpreted; see each reason below.

swi-definition.name: eXML_SetOption
swi-definition.description: Set the number of spaces used to indent nested elements

entry.register-use: number of spaces to indent by, or 0 to disable indenting

use.p: To produce readable XML output, eXML indents nested elements. This preference sets the number of spaces used per nesting level; the default is 2. Setting it to 0 disables indenting entirely.

p.extended-example: <?xml version="1.0" encoding="ISO-8859-1"?> <page type="Page" category="Test" name="1" fileType="CNDoc"> <begin> <transition name="Dissolve"> <parameters> <speed>Fast</speed> </parameters> </transition> </begin> </page>

swi-definition.name: eXML_SetOption
swi-definition.description: Set the depth up to which extra blank lines are inserted before elements

entry.register-use: deepest nesting level, counting from 1, at which an extra blank line is inserted before an element; 0 to disable

use.p: Readability can be further improved by inserting a blank line before the opening tag of higher-level elements. By default, extra lines are only inserted at the first nesting level; setting this to 2 or 3 extends that to deeper levels.

swi-definition.name: eXML_SetOption
swi-definition.description: Set the character used to terminate strings returned by the module

entry.register-use: ASCII value of the terminating character

use.p: By default, every string returned by eXML is terminated with a 0x00 byte, suiting C and Assembler. BASIC programs need a 0x0D (Carriage Return) terminator instead; use this preference to change it. The change affects only later calls made with this workspace pointer in R0.

swi-definition.name: eXML_SetOption
swi-definition.description: Set the character used to separate element names in a context string

entry.register-use: ASCII value of the separator character, or a string whose first character is used

use.p: , and the string form of context returned by , join element names with / by default, eg. /document/chapter/page/frame. This preference selects a different separator character. Avoid choosing a character that can legally appear inside an element name.

swi-definition.name: eXML_SetOption
swi-definition.description: Set the character used to separate an element's context from an attribute name

entry.register-use: ASCII value of the separator character, or a string whose first character is used

use.p: This preference works like , but for addressing an attribute within an element's opening tag, eg. /document/chapter/page@print to address the print attribute of that page element, once @ has been set as the attribute separator.

swi-definition.name: eXML_SetOption
swi-definition.description: Set the RISC OS filetype used for files created by the module

use.p: By default, XML files created by eXML are typed as Text (&hex;FFF), so they can be checked in a standard text editor such as !Edit, !StrongEd or !Zap. This preference sets an alternative filetype, such as &hex;F80 (XML), to be applied when the file is closed. It only affects files being created; it is ignored when reading an existing file.

swi-definition.name: eXML_SetOption
swi-definition.description: Set the directory used for the temporary file created when updating an XML file

entry.register-use: pointer to a directory path string

use.p: may need to create a temporary file. By default, eXML uses <Wimp$ScrapDir> (creating an eXML subdirectory within it), falling back to <eXML$Dir>.Scrap if that variable cannot be accessed. This preference selects a different directory.

swi-definition.name: eXML_ClearAttributes
swi-definition.description: Clear the pending attribute stack

use.p: Clears the stack of attributes accumulated by . The stack is cleared automatically once a new element is created, so this call is rarely needed; it exists for the case where the state of the stack is uncertain, for example after an error.

section.title: SWI Calls: Reading (Parsing) an XML File

swi-definition.name: eXML_ParseBuffer
swi-definition.description: Present an XML document already held in memory to the parser

entry.register-use: size of the data, in bytes

use.p: The simplest way to parse an XML file is to load it entirely into a buffer in the application's own memory and hand that buffer to eXML with this call, then parse it with repeated calls to . This only works when the file's size is known and it is small enough to hold in memory, which is true of most everyday XML files.

p.extended-example: SYS "OS_File",17,"adfs::4.$.TestFile" TO type%,,,,xml_len% IF type% = 0 THEN ERROR 1,"No such file" DIM xml_buf% xml_len% OSCLI "LOAD "+xml$+" "+STR$~(xml_buf%) SYS "eXML_ParseBuffer",xml%,xml_buf%,xml_len%

swi-definition.name: eXML_ParseFile
swi-definition.description: Open an XML file to be read, a character at a time, by the parser

entry.register-use:
Flags:
A leading <?xml?> header is required Accept a file without a proper <?xml?> header; only the first character of the file is then checked, and must be a "<"

exit.register-use: handle of the opened file, or 0 if it could not be opened

use.p: Use this call instead of when a file is too large to hold in memory, or when its size is not known in advance, such as when parsing streamed data. The file is read a character at a time as parsing proceeds. As with , call repeatedly until parsing is finished.

p.extended-example:
SYS "eXML_InitBuffer" TO size% DIM xml% size% SYS "eXML_InitBuffer",xml%
SYS "eXML_SetOption",xml%,eXML_Option_Terminator,13 SYS "eXML_SetOption",xml%,eXML_Option_Separator,"/"
SYS "eXML_ParseFile",xml%,"adfs::4.$.MyFile" TO in%
REPEAT SYS "eXML_Parse",xml%,0 TO r%,element%,attr%,context% CASE r% OF WHEN eXML_Parser_Start PRINT "S/"+$element% WHEN eXML_Parser_End PRINT "E/"+$element% WHEN eXML_Parser_ERROR PRINT "ERROR !!!" ENDCASE UNTIL r% = eXML_Parser_Finished OR r% = eXML_Parser_ERROR
SYS "eXML_Close",xml%

swi-definition.name: eXML_Parse
swi-definition.description: Continue parsing an XML document, one syntactic event at a time

entry.register-use: mask; not used at present, should be 0

Flags:
Return a context array in R3 on exit (see context array) Return a context string in R3 on exit (see context string) Report an error for badly structured XML Don't escape special characters, and don't produce an error for badly structured input; useful when parsing simple HTML, which may nest elements improperly, but should never be set when parsing genuine XML

value-table.value: Null - no event to report; call Wimp_Poll and call this SWI again, to allow multitasking to continue whilst parsing a large file
Start - a StartElement was found (R1 -> element name)
End - an EndElement was found (R1 -> element name)
Content - content was found (R1 -> content, R2 = number of bytes to read)
Declaration - a declaration was found, eg. <?xat creator="MyProg" version="4.0"?> (R1 -> declaration name)
PI - a Processing Instruction was found
DTD - a DOCTYPE definition was found; see (R1 -> undecoded DTD data)
Finished - parsing has finished (from version 0.22 onwards, R1 = number of bytes read)
ERROR - an error occurred during parsing (R1 = row, R2 = column of the last element encountered before the error)
Encoding - the requested encoding is not known or not supported

exit.register-use: pointer to the current element name, for the codes noted above; terminated with the configured terminator (see )
pointer to an attribute array, or 0 if there are no attributes, for Start and Declaration
pointer to a context array or context string, depending on bit 0 of the flags on entry

use.p: Once the workspace has been initialised and a document has been presented with or , call this SWI repeatedly to parse it, until it returns the Finished or ERROR code. eXML tracks the exact position reached within the document; to restart parsing from the beginning, present the document again with or .
Your application need not respond to every return code - many can safely be ignored - but it must always respond to ERROR and Finished, so that the parsing loop terminates.

A self-closing element, eg. <colour type="rgb" value="255,255,255" />, always produces a Start code immediately followed by an End code, so that calling code can track nesting depth itself without special-casing self-closing elements.

When content is found, R1 points to the data and R2 gives the number of bytes to read; a suitable terminator is always present at the byte immediately following the data, so a short string of content can be read directly as a terminated string. The content may arrive as a single block, or scattered across a series of Content events, depending on the available buffer space and the transport in use; calling code should be able to cope with content arriving in several pieces.

p.extended-example:
SYS "eXML_ParseBuffer",xml%,xml_buf%,xml_len%
REPEAT SYS "eXML_Parse",xml%,0 TO r%,element%,attr% CASE r% OF WHEN eXML_Parser_Start PRINT "S/"+$element% WHEN eXML_Parser_End PRINT "E/"+$element% WHEN eXML_Parser_ERROR PRINT "ERROR !!!" ENDCASE UNTIL r% = eXML_Parser_Finished OR r% = eXML_Parser_ERROR

swi-definition.name: eXML_Context
swi-definition.description: Return the current parse position as a single context string

entry.register-use: pointer to a separator string, or 0 to use the default separator ("/")

exit.register-use: pointer to the context string

use.p: can return the current context as an array of element-name pointers (see context array); this call instead builds a single, user-readable context string on demand, useful when Content has just been reported and the calling code wants to know which series of elements it belongs to.

The returned string is terminated with the configured terminator (see ). As with the context array, the name of the element currently being opened or closed is not included, since it is not yet (or no longer) part of the context at that point.

p.extended-example: REPEAT SYS "eXML_Parse",xml% TO r%,element%,attr% SYS "eXML_Context",xml%,"/" TO context$ PRINT context$ UNTIL eXML_Parser_Finished

swi-definition.name: eXML_DecodeDTD
swi-definition.description: Decode a DOCTYPE declaration into its constituent parts

entry.register-use: pointer to the DTD line's contents, as returned by

exit.register-use: 0 if successful, else -> error block
pointer to the document-type (a string containing no spaces)
pointer to the identifier string
pointer to the URL
undefined at present; reserved for future use

Updated flags:
The declaration is SYSTEM (local) The declaration is PUBLIC (external), rather than SYSTEM

use.p: A well-formed XML document should contain a Document Type Declaration (DTD), usually near the start of the file, so that its structure and syntax can be verified against a set of rules, for example:

Because the syntax of a DTD line is quite free-form - it may, for instance, be spread over several lines - this call decodes it into the useful parts listed above. Document creation code is encouraged to build such lines with instead of constructing them by hand, as that ensures correct syntax.

There is no support at present for an embedded (in-line) DTD; only a reference to an external DTD file (whether local, SYSTEM, or public, PUBLIC) is decoded. As in-line DTDs are being phased out in favour of XML Schema, it is unlikely that support will be added.
The presence of the referenced DTD file is not checked by eXML: the URL is supplied purely for the benefit of an external XML validation tool, and by convention uses a .dtd filename extension.

swi-definition.name: eXML_DecodeString
swi-definition.description: Convert an XML-escaped string back into plain ASCII text

exit.register-use: preserved
pointer to the terminating NULL in the destination buffer

use.p: Performs the reverse operation to : it copies the source string to the destination, translating each escape sequence (&lt;, &gt;, &amp;, &apos;, &quot;) back into the corresponding ISO Latin-1 character.

swi-definition.name: eXML_Pointer
swi-definition.description: Read the parser's current position within the document

exit.register-use: offset into the buffer (or file) holding the document

use.p: Added in version 0.36. This call reads the parser's current position, allowing an application to record the start and end points of the content held within an element, so that the sub-content between those points can be parsed or otherwise processed again later.

section.title: SWI Calls: Writing an XML File

swi-definition.name: eXML_Open
swi-definition.description: Create a new XML file and write its XML declaration

entry.register-use: pointer to an attribute array, or 0
pointer to a version string, or 0
pointer to an encoding string, or 0

Flags:
Write the <?xml?> header as usual Do not write the <?xml?> header

exit.register-use: file handle, or 0 if not successful

use.p: As part of opening the file, this call writes the XML declaration as the first line of the file, eg. <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>. The version and encoding attributes may be supplied directly in R3 and R4 (the common case, since both are more or less mandatory), or as ordinary attributes in the array pointed to by R2 - or a mixture of the two, though R2 may be 0 if only version and encoding are required. R2, R3 and R4 are all optional and should be 0 if not used.
The call returns the handle of the newly opened file (or 0 on failure), so that the caller can track it and close it if an error occurs partway through writing.

swi-definition.name: eXML_OpenFile
swi-definition.description: Alternative spelling for eXML_Open

use.p: This call behaves identically to ; see that entry for its registers and use.

swi-definition.name: eXML_OpenBuffer
swi-definition.description: Begin a new XML document written to a buffer in memory, rather than a file

entry.register-use: pointer to a buffer to hold the data; the first word of the buffer must hold its size
pointer to an attribute array, or 0
pointer to a version string, or 0
pointer to an encoding string, or 0

Flags:
Write the <?xml?> header as usual Do not write the <?xml?> header

exit.register-use: error code (0 if OK)

use.p: Works in the same way as , except that all further output is written into the supplied memory buffer rather than to a file. This is useful, for example, when building a header for streamed (eg. internet) communication that does not need to be saved to disc first.

swi-definition.name: eXML_Close
swi-definition.description: Close a file previously opened for writing

entry.register-use: RISC OS filetype to give the file, or 0 to use the currently configured filetype (see )

exit.register-use: pointer to the buffer, if was used to create the file (otherwise preserved)
number of bytes written, if was used to create the file (otherwise preserved)
size of the buffer given in R0, if was used to create the file (otherwise preserved)

use.p: Closes the file most recently opened with or , and clears the module's internal pointers to it. If it was opened as a file, the filetype given in R1 (or the configured default, Text &hex;FFF, if R1 is 0) is applied. The filetype is only used when writing; it has no effect when reading an existing XML file.

swi-definition.name: eXML_UpdateBuffer
swi-definition.description: Open an in-memory XML document for selective update

use.p: Not yet implemented.

swi-definition.name: eXML_UpdateFile
swi-definition.description: Open an existing XML file for selective update

exit.register-use: filehandle of the input file, or 0 if not successful
filehandle of the output file, or 0 if not successful

use.p: In some situations, an application needs to update only part of an existing XML file, for example one that several applications share. This call opens an existing file (creating a new output file alongside it) so that its content can be scanned for a required element; the caller's own data can then be inserted, the original element skipped, and scanning continued. Once opened, call repeatedly until parsing is finished, in the same way as .

p.extended-example:
SYS "eXML_Init" TO size% DIM xml% size% SYS "eXML_Init",xml%
SYS "eXML_SetOption",xml%,eXML_Option_Terminator,13 SYS "eXML_SetOption",xml%,eXML_Option_Separator,"/"
SYS "eXML_UpdateFile",xml%,"adfs::4.$.MyFile" TO in%,out%
claim% = 0 REPEAT SYS "eXML_Update",xml%,,,,,claim% TO r%,,,context$ claim% = 0 CASE r% OF WHEN eXML_Parser_Start CASE context$ OF WHEN "/document/chapter/page" claim% = 1 ENDCASE WHEN eXML_Parser_ERROR PRINT "!!! Parser ERROR !!!" ENDCASE UNTIL r% = eXML_Parser_Finished OR r% = eXML_Parser_ERROR
SYS "eXML_Close",xml%,FileType_XML

swi-definition.name: eXML_Update
swi-definition.description: Continue a selective update of an XML file previously opened for update

entry.register-use:
Flags: on the first call, bit 0 must be clear.
Leave the current element unclaimed Claim the previous element (and everything within it): it will be skipped, and no further elements within it will be reported, until it has closed When claiming, claim only the opening tag of the element, so it can be replaced by an updated one

register-use.p: Return code (a subset of those used by ; only these are returned):

value-table.value: ERROR - an error occurred during parsing

exit.register-use: pointer to the name of the last element
pointer to an attribute array of the last element
pointer to an expanded context string, which - unlike 's context - includes the name of the current element

use.p: Call this SWI repeatedly, after opening a file with or , until parsing has finished. Once the expanded context string in R3 matches the element you were looking for, set bit 0 of the flags on the next call to claim that element (and everything nested within it): it is skipped, and no further elements within it are reported, until it has closed.

swi-definition.name: eXML_StartElement
swi-definition.description: Write the opening tag of a new element

entry.register-use: pointer to the element name (optionally prefixed with "/" to mark it self-closing; see below)
pointer to an attribute array, or 0
pointer to a content string, or 0

Flags:
A normal element, requiring a matching This is an empty (self-closing) element; do not call for it Insert a line feed at the end of this tag Don't insert a line feed at the end of this tag Indent this element with leading spaces, as normal Don't indent this element (no leading spaces before the tag) Keep all attributes on the same line as the tag Start each attribute on a new line, to improve readability

exit.register-use: 0 if successful, else -> error block

use.p: Writes the opening tag of a new element to the file (or buffer) opened by or . A StartElement should normally be followed by optional content, optional nested elements, and finally a matching .

An element may instead be marked empty (self-closing), in which case it may still hold attributes but cannot hold content or nested elements, and a / is inserted before the tag's closing >, eg. <colour red="255" green="128" blue="44"/>. An element can be marked self-closing in any of three ways: by setting bit 0 of the flags on entry; by prefixing the element name in R1 with /, eg. R1 -> /colour; or by supplying a content string in R3 (see below). In every case, do not call for the element - it is closed automatically.

A single short line of text can be inserted as content by pointing R3 at it: the StartElement is written, the content is inserted, and the EndElement is written automatically, so no separate call to is required. For example:
produces:
If more than one line of text is needed, omit the string in R3 and use between matching and calls instead.

swi-definition.name: eXML_EndElement
swi-definition.description: Write the closing tag of an element previously opened with eXML_StartElement

entry.register-use: pointer to the element name, or 0 to close the most recently opened element

Flags:
Insert a line feed after this element, as normal Don't insert a line feed after this element Indent as normal (leading spaces before the tag) Don't indent (no leading spaces before the tag)

exit.register-use: 0 if successful, else -> error block

use.p: Closes an element previously opened with - except an element that was marked self-closing, which must not be closed explicitly. Every other opened element must eventually be closed, and elements must be closed in the correct (nested) order; XML does not permit overlapping elements.

eXML checks the element name given in R1 against its internal stack of open elements, and produces an error if the wrong element is closed. Supplying 0 in R1 closes the most recently opened element without this check, but this is not recommended, since it prevents eXML from verifying that elements are being closed in the correct order.

whilst this produces an error, because <frame> and <page> close in the wrong order:

swi-definition.name: eXML_Content
swi-definition.description: Write content data inside the currently open element

entry.register-use:
Flags:
Insert a line feed after the data, as normal Don't insert a line feed after the data Insert leading white space before the output, as normal Don't insert leading white space before the output Translate reserved characters, as normal Don't translate reserved (special) characters

exit.register-use: 0 if successful, else -> error block

use.p: Inserts content inside the element most recently opened with . A single short line can also be supplied directly to ; use this call instead for larger blocks of text, multiple lines, or any number of bytes. Content may contain line feed and/or carriage return characters, and these are preserved (unlike in HTML).
Content may only be written once an element is open; writing content without an open element produces the error.

example.p: The following places content inside a nested element:

swi-definition.name: eXML_Attribute
swi-definition.description: Add one attribute to the pending attribute stack

exit.register-use: pointer to an attribute array, or 0 if unsuccessful

use.p: An attribute takes the form name="value", and an element may carry any number of them. Rather than building an attribute array by hand, call this SWI once for each attribute to be added to the pending stack, then pass the returned pointer to , , or . The stack is cleared automatically once the element is created, so it rarely needs to be cleared explicitly (see ).

p.extended-example: SYS "eXML_StartElement",xml%,"document" id$ = "1" value$ = "date and time" SYS "eXML_Attribute",xml%,"id",id$ TO attr% SYS "eXML_Attribute",xml%,"name",value$ TO attr% SYS "eXML_StartElement",xml%,"field",attr%,"Hello" SYS "eXML_EndElement",xml%,"document"

example.p: Note that the field element does not need an explicit call, since it was given a content string and so is closed automatically.

swi-definition.name: eXML_Declaration
swi-definition.description: Write a processing declaration, such as the leading <?xml?> declaration

entry.register-use: pointer to an attribute array, or 0

exit.register-use: pointer to an attribute array, or 0 if unsuccessful

use.p: Declarations are typically used near the start of a document; the most common is the <?xml?> declaration, which must be present for a document to be considered valid. This call produces output similar to , but the line begins with <? and ends with ?>. Declarations do not need to be (and cannot be) closed with , and are not considered part of the document body.
The content and processing of a declaration is entirely up to the application reading it; eXML places no further interpretation on it.

swi-definition.name: eXML_Comment
swi-definition.description: Write a comment

entry.register-use: length of the string in R1, or 0 to use the entire string up to a control character

exit.register-use: 0 if successful, else Corrupted

use.p: Writes a comment to the output document, in the standard form <!-- comment text -->.

p.extended-example: SYS "eXML_Comment",xml%,"this is a comment" SYS "eXML_Comment",xml%,"this is a comment",17

swi-definition.name: eXML_DTD
swi-definition.description: Write a DOCTYPE declaration

entry.register-use: pointer to an identifier string (optional, PUBLIC only)

Flags:
Insert white space before this element, as normal Don't insert white space before this element The DTD is SYSTEM (local) The DTD is PUBLIC, rather than SYSTEM Information from the DTD is included in-line (not currently supported)

exit.register-use: 0 if successful, else -> error block

use.p: Writes a DOCTYPE line at the start of a document, after the <?xml?> declaration but before the first element. A DTD describes the structure of a document, and the possible values for each attribute, so that a validation tool can check the document against it; it is also used by the XML File Dispatcher to identify a document's type when it is double-clicked.

There are three kinds of DTD. A SYSTEM DTD is stored locally, and needs only a relative URL to the DTD file in R3. A PUBLIC DTD is stored externally (for example on the internet); it needs a URL in R3 and an identifier string in R2 describing the publisher, format and language of the document, and is selected by setting bit 4 of the flags. An in-line DTD embeds its information directly in the DOCTYPE declaration, but this is not currently supported by eXML.

The document-type in R1 identifies the kind of document, eg. svg; where an application uses several document types, including the application's own name as a prefix, eg. artworks:svg, allows an unlimited number of distinct types to be created without clashing with anyone else's.

The identifier in R2 (PUBLIC DTDs only) should describe the publisher, the document format and version, and the language, separated by double forward-slashes, eg. -//XAT//CableNews Edition 4.0//EN. A leading - indicates a publisher that is not ISO certified; a leading + indicates one that is. A SYSTEM DTD has no identifier; if one is supplied it is ignored, so that XML checkers and browsers do not report an error over it.

The URL in R3 is not used by eXML's own parser: it exists purely for an external XML validation tool. For a SYSTEM DTD, use a relative path, eg. edition.dtd or files/edition.dtd; for a PUBLIC DTD, use an absolute URL, eg. http://www.xat.nl/dtd/cablenews/edition.dtd. In both cases the filename should carry a .dtd extension, and the path should be given in URL form rather than RISC OS pathname form.

swi-definition.name: eXML_PI
swi-definition.description: Write a Processing Instruction

exit.register-use: 0 if successful, else -> error block

use.p: Inserts a Processing Instruction into the output document, used to pass information directly to whatever XML processor reads the document (for example, the parser inside your own application). Processing instructions are not considered part of the document body, and their syntax is not checked by eXML. Only the opening (<?) and closing (?>) delimiters are added; the data in R1 is inserted between them exactly as supplied.

swi-definition.name: eXML_CDATA
swi-definition.description: Write a CDATA (raw data) section

exit.register-use: 0 if successful, else -> error block

use.p: The XML standard allows raw data - including reserved characters such as < and > - to be inserted into a document without escaping, inside a CDATA section. The only sequence a CDATA section cannot contain is ]]>, which marks its end. A CDATA section is opened with <![CDATA[ and closed with ]]>.
Reading CDATA sections is not currently supported by eXML.

section.title: SWI Calls: Universal Calls

swi-definition.name: eXML_GetString
swi-definition.description: Copy a control-terminated string, applying a chosen terminator

entry.register-use: pointer to the destination, somewhere in the caller's own workspace

exit.register-use: pointer to the terminating character written into the destination string
length of the destination string, excluding its terminator

use.p: This call is not really specific to XML, but is provided because it is useful for building structures (such as large menus) from data received elsewhere, for example a WIMP message. It copies a string terminated by any control character into the caller's own buffer, applying whichever terminator the caller's software requires.

example.p: The following, in BBC BASIC, extracts the document-type and path from a message block:

p.extended-example: DIM mes 256 DIM par% 256 ... SYS "eXML_GetString",mes!40,par%,13 doctype$ = $par% SYS "eXML_GetString",mes+44,par%,13 path$ = $par%

swi-definition.name: eXML_ColourOp
swi-definition.description: Read, write, and convert between colour formats

use.p: There are many ways to express a colour in an XML document - some inherited from HTML, some specific to XML - and converting between them can be tedious, especially when the user should be free to choose their preferred colour model. converts between these formats, and reads or writes colours directly. Every reason code operates on a colour data block held in the caller's own memory (except reason codes 3 and 4, which use the module's own internal workspace instead - see below). R0 selects the operation; the meaning of the other registers depends on the reason code.

It is recommended that colour be expressed as an attribute on an existing element rather than as an element of its own, eg. <background colour="rgb(255,255,255)"/> rather than <background><colour value="rgb(255,255,255)"/></background>.

swi-definition.name: eXML_ColourOp
swi-definition.description: Initialise a colour data block, or find its required size

entry.register-use: pointer to a colour data block, or 0 to find the required size

Flags:
Required string terminator, eg. 0 or 13

exit.register-use: size of the colour data block, in bytes, when R1 was 0 on entry

use.p: Before a colour data block is used with any other reason code, it should be set to a defined state by calling this reason code with a pointer to it in R1. To find the required size of the block, call with a null pointer in R1; the size is returned in R2. The size should always be requested first, since it may grow in a future version of the module.

swi-definition.name: eXML_ColourOp
swi-definition.description: Read a colour from a text string into a colour data block

entry.register-use: pointer to a colour data block
pointer to a text string containing a colour definition

use.p: Parses the colour definition string in R2, in any of the formats described under colour data block, and updates the block pointed to by R1 with the resulting colour, colour model, and format.

swi-definition.name: eXML_ColourOp
swi-definition.description: Write a colour data block out as a formatted text string

entry.register-use: pointer to a colour data block
pointer to a buffer to hold the resulting string

Flags:
Required string terminator, eg. 0 or 13 Required output colour format (see colour data block); 0 to use the format already recorded in the block

use.p: Formats the colour held in the data block pointed to by R1 as text, in either the colour's original format or the format requested in bits 8-15 of the flags, and writes it to the buffer in R2. This is typically used directly to produce XML output.

p.extended-example:
SYS "eXML_ColourOp",0,0 TO ,,size% DIM block% size% DIM string% 256
SYS "eXML_ColourOp",0,block%
SYS "eXML_ColourOp",2,block%,string%,,,13 OR (2 << 8) PRINT $string%
SYS "eXML_ColourOp",1,block%,string% PRINT ~block%!12

swi-definition.name: eXML_ColourOp
swi-definition.description: Convert a colour string directly into a RISC OS colour value

entry.register-use: pointer to a formatted colour text string

exit.register-use: the colour, as a RISC OS colour value

use.p: Equivalent to , but uses the module's own internal workspace for the conversion rather than a caller-supplied colour data block, so no block needs to be created first.

swi-definition.name: eXML_ColourOp
swi-definition.description: Convert a RISC OS colour value directly into a formatted text string

entry.register-use: colour value, in RISC OS format

exit.register-use: pointer to the resulting string

use.p: Equivalent to , but uses the module's own internal workspace for the conversion rather than a caller-supplied colour data block.

swi-definition.name: eXML_DateOp
swi-definition.description: Read (and, in future, write) dates and times in various formats

register-use.p: Format to read (or, when writing, to produce):

value-table.value: XML - year-month-date, separated by dashes, eg. 2016-12-31
EUR - date-month-year, separated by dashes, eg. 31-12-2016
USA - month/date/year, separated by slashes, eg. 12/31/2016

register-use.p: When writing (not yet implemented), further flags select what is written:

bitfield-table.bit: Write a date (rather than read one)

use.p: The official XML standard specifies dates in reverse (year-month-date) order, separated by dashes, eg. 2014-06-31, optionally followed by a time, separated by an optional space and the letter T, eg. 2014-06-31 T14:23:01. The part following T gives hours, minutes and seconds, each separated by a colon.

Reading is implemented: this call reads an existing date (and optional time) from a text string, either in a specific format selected in R0, or automatically (format 0), in which case XML and EUR dates are assumed to be separated by dashes and USA dates by slashes. Writing a date is not yet implemented.

swi-definition.name: eXML_EncodeString
swi-definition.description: Copy a NULL-terminated string, escaping reserved XML characters

exit.register-use: preserved
pointer to the terminating NULL in the destination buffer

use.p: Copies a NULL-terminated string from the source in R0 to the destination in R1, translating any of the reserved characters (<, >, &, ', ") into the corresponding XML escape sequence (&lt;, &gt;, &amp;, &apos;, &quot;).

swi-definition.name: eXML_Base64
swi-definition.description: Encode or decode Base64 data

use.p: Not implemented.

section.p: The eXML module distributed as version 0.43 (13 Jun 2020) - one point release after this API document - also occupies four further SWI numbers in its decoding table which this specification does not describe: eXML_GetStack (&hex;576D9), eXML_ConvertToUTF8 (&hex;576DA), eXML_DecodeBlock (&hex;576E2), and eXML_Debug (&hex;576E3). Their names are known from the module's own SWI decoding table, but their calling conventions are not published anywhere, so they are not documented as full SWI entries here.

section.title: XML File Dispatcher
section.p: Most files on RISC OS carry a filetype, which lets an application recognise its own files and respond when the Filer reports that one has been double-clicked; if no application claims a filetype, the Filer falls back to a system variable such as Alias$@RunType_FFF to launch something suitable.

XML makes it easy to create many new file formats, but RISC OS filetypes are a scarce resource (numbers &hex;000 to &hex;FFF only), and typically only one filetype will be allocated to a given application, which must then inspect each file's contents to work out how to use it. By default, an XML file with no more specific filetype allocated to it should use RISC OS filetype &hex;F80. Although every such file then looks identical to the Filer, its document-type can still be recovered from its DOCTYPE line, eg.

p.extended-example: <?xml version="1.0" encoding="ISO-8859-1"?> <!DOCTYPE MyDoc SYSTEM "mydoc.dtd"> <document> <chapter id="1"> <page id="1"> <frame>Hello world...</frame> </page> </chapter> </document>

section.p: Here, the document-type (referred to below as <doctype>) is MyDoc. A document-type may be any length and contain any printable XML character except a space; conventionally it uses only letters and, perhaps, numbers, eg. artworks, svg, cablenews, config. An application handling several distinct document-types of its own may prefix them with a family name and a colon, eg. artworks:config, but should only do this for a format that is intended to remain private, rather than public - see also below.

For any of this to work, the file must carry RISC OS filetype &hex;F80. Double-clicking such a file is intercepted by eXML, which extracts the document-type from its DOCTYPE line and then either broadcasts a WIMP message, or launches a suitable application, as described below.

section.title: XML File Dispatcher: System Variables
section.p: eXML uses system variables of the following form to decide what to launch when an XML file is opened:

sysvar-definition.name: XML$@Run_<doctype>
sysvar-definition.description: Command used to launch an application for a given XML document-type

use.p: An application which wants to be launched automatically whenever the user double-clicks a file of a given <doctype> should set this variable, replacing <doctype> with the actual document-type it handles, to a command that launches it with the file's pathname in its command tail:

example.p: Note the doubled %, which is required to escape the literal % that follows it. Whenever the user double-clicks an XML file (RISC OS filetype &hex;F80) with document-type svg, and ArtWorks is not already running, eXML launches it as configured, substituting the file's pathname for %*0 in the command tail.

section.p: If no XML$@Run_<doctype> variable exists for a file's document-type, and no running application claims the message described below, the file cannot be opened automatically. Every other system variable beginning XML$@ is reserved for future use by eXML.

section.title: XML File Dispatcher: Messages
section.p: Before falling back to the XML$@Run_<doctype> system variable, the dispatcher broadcasts a User_Message (18) of type , in a format similar to the standard Message_DataOpen (5) broadcast by the Filer when any file is double-clicked. The only difference is that the field at offset +40 holds a pointer to a string giving the document-type, rather than the filetype.

message-definition.name: XMLDataOpen
message-definition.description: A user has double-clicked an XML file of the given document-type

message-table.message: The sender's reference for this message
Window handle of the directory display containing the file
X offset of the file icon that was double-clicked
Y offset of the file icon that was double-clicked
Pointer to a zero-terminated string giving the document-type
Full pathname of the file, zero-terminated

use.p: Any application that can load a file of the document-type given at offset +40 should respond by first claiming the message - by sending a reply, with your_ref set to the original message's my_ref - and only then loading the file. Claiming first, before attempting to load, avoids the message being passed on to another application if the load subsequently fails.

p.extended-example:
DIM mes 256 ... REPEAT SYS "Wimp_Poll", 0, mes TO r% CASE r% OF WHEN 17, 18, 19 : PROC_message ENDCASE UNTIL quit
DEF PROC_message CASE mes!16 OF WHEN &40D59 : PROC_xml_dataopen ENDCASE ENDPROC
DEF PROC_xml_dataopen doctype$ = FN_read_string(mes!40) file$ = FNread_string(mes+44) CASE doctype$ OF WHEN "svg" mes!16 = &40D5A mes!12 = mes!8 SYS "Wimp_SendMessage",17,mes,mes!4 REM ---> load the file ... ENDCASE ENDPROC

message-definition.name: XMLDataOpenAck
message-definition.description: Acknowledges and claims a XMLDataOpen message

use.p: Sent as a User_Message (17) reply to , with your_ref copied from the original message's my_ref, to claim the file before loading it.

section.title: XML File Dispatcher: Naming Conventions
section.p: Choose a document-type carefully, to avoid clashing with another application's document-type when a file is loaded automatically. Prefer a name qualified by your own application or company, such as MyApp:MyDoc or MyCompany:MyDoc, over an unqualified name such as MyDoc. Some examples: artworks, xat:database, dbman:users, xat:dbman:database.

error-definition.name: eXML_FileNotOpen
error-definition.description: A call that writes to, or reads the position of, an XML file was made with no file currently open

use.p: Returned by any call that writes content, elements, or other output when no file (or buffer) is currently open for writing, for example calling before or .

error-definition.name: eXML_NoElement
error-definition.description: An operation on an element was requested, but no element is currently open

use.p: Returned, for example, by when there is no corresponding open element left to close.

error-definition.name: eXML_NoEnd
error-definition.description: More elements were closed than have been opened

use.p: Returned by when trying to close an element after every currently open element has already been closed.

error-definition.name: eXML_WrongEnd
error-definition.description: An element was closed with a name that does not match the most recently opened element

use.p: Returned by when the element name given in R1 does not match the element eXML expects to be closed next, according to its internal stack of open elements - for example, closing elements in the wrong (non-nested) order.

error-definition.name: eXML_NoEncoding
error-definition.description: The requested character encoding is not known, or is not supported by this version of the module

use.p: Returned by (as the Encoding return code) when a document requests an encoding outside the set listed under , or one that is not yet implemented in the running version of the module.

error-definition.name: eXML_NoDocType
error-definition.description: An operation on a DOCTYPE declaration was requested, but no document-type could be determined

use.p: Returned when a document-type cannot be established from a DOCTYPE declaration, for example when dispatching a double-clicked XML file, or when decoding a malformed DTD line with .

error-definition.name: eXML_Despatch
error-definition.description: The XML File Dispatcher could not dispatch a double-clicked file

use.p: Returned when the XML File Dispatcher cannot dispatch a double-clicked XML file - for example, no application claimed the message, and no matching XML$@Run_<doctype> system variable was set.

error-definition.name: eXML_Workspace
error-definition.description: The workspace pointer supplied in R0 is not valid, or has not been initialised

use.p: Returned when a call is made with a workspace pointer that eXML does not recognise as having been initialised by or .

error-definition.name: eXML_Buffer
error-definition.description: No content buffer is available, or the supplied buffer pointer is not valid

use.p: Returned when a call needs the workspace's Content buffer (see ), but none is available, or when a caller-supplied buffer pointer, for example to , is not valid.

error-definition.name: eXML_BufferSize
error-definition.description: The supplied buffer is too small for the data being read or written

use.p: Returned when a caller-supplied buffer, such as the Content buffer sized by , or the buffer given to , is too small to hold the data eXML needs to read or write into it.

error-definition.name: eXML_ColourUnknown
error-definition.description: A colour string uses a format that is not recognised

use.p: Returned by (or reason 3) when the text supplied does not match any of the colour formats described under colour data block.

error-definition.name: eXML_ColourSyntax
error-definition.description: A colour string is in a recognised format, but is not syntactically valid

use.p: Returned by (or reason 3) when the text supplied is recognisably one of the supported colour formats, but its syntax is malformed - for example, a missing value or an unmatched bracket.

error-definition.name: eXML_ColourFormat
error-definition.description: The requested output colour format is not supported for writing

use.p: Returned by (or reason 4) when the colour format requested in the flags is one that the module does not yet support producing, such as YUV or YUV%.

error-definition.name: eXML_ColourValue
error-definition.description: A colour value cannot be converted into the requested format or model

use.p: Returned by (or reason 4) when the stored colour value cannot be represented in the requested output format, for example because it falls outside the range that format can express.
